findings.passage: “Ensuring that only eligible citizens cast a ballot is vital to protecting the integrity of our elections, and Arizona has long been a national leader on this issue. I am proud to defend Arizona’s laws at the Supreme Court.”
findings.note: Her quote in an Attorney General's office press release announcing a brief at the U.S. Supreme Court defending Arizona's proof-of-citizenship requirement for people registering on the state form. The release also quotes her saying Arizona has clear authority to make sure the people registering to vote here are actually eligible.

findings.passage: In fact, Arizona already requires documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote.
findings.note: From a statement issued in her name replying to a federal official's remarks about Arizona elections. The same statement says voter fraud is exceedingly rare and has not played a meaningful role in the outcome of an election.

findings.motion: Attorney General Opinion I24-015 (R24-015), treatment of state voter registration forms not accompanied by documentary proof of citizenship
findings.note: Opinion issued by her to the Secretary of State. It says county recorders should run the standard motor-vehicle database check for proof of citizenship before rejecting a state form, and that missing proof may be supplied until 7:00 p.m. on election day.

findings.motion: Attorney General Opinion I25-007 (R25-009), voters with legacy driver-license records and proof of citizenship
findings.note: Opinion issued by her to the Secretary of State. It says county recorders may ask affected voters for satisfactory evidence of citizenship but may not cancel a registration merely because of a records error or because the voter does not respond.

findings.motion: Joined multistate lawsuit over Executive Order 14248, including its documentary-proof-of-citizenship requirement for military and overseas voters
findings.note: Her office announced she joined 19 states suing over the order. The release challenges the provision requiring military and overseas voters to submit documentary proof of citizenship, saying the federal form has no such requirement.

findings.passage: I believe this Rule is within the ATF’s authority and provides much-needed regulation of ghost guns, which have proliferated in recent years and have made law enforcement’s job more difficult and dangerous,
findings.note: Statement of the Attorney General in her office's press release announcing Arizona's withdrawal from a multistate lawsuit against the federal agency's rule covering privately made firearms and parts kits.

findings.motion: Withdrawal of Arizona from multistate lawsuit challenging the federal ATF rule on ghost guns (privately made firearms and parts kits)
findings.note: The Attorney General withdrew the state from a lawsuit filed in July 2022 by the prior administration; the rule defines 'firearm' to include privately made firearms and easily assembled parts kits.

findings.passage: “Protecting our communities from gun violence requires multiple solutions, including laws already on the books,” said Attorney General Mayes. “For nearly 60 years, federal law has prohibited the sale of handguns from federally licensed dealers to individuals under 21. The Second Amendment allows for such age-based restrictions, and I urge the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit to affirm the district court ruling and allow this critical safeguard to stand.”
findings.note: Statement of the Attorney General in her office's press release (dated 2023-05-24) on the amicus brief filed the week before.
subjects: minimum age to buy a gun

findings.motion: Joined 21-attorney-general amicus brief, Reese v. ATF (5th Cir.), supporting the federal ban on handgun sales by licensed dealers to people under 21
findings.note: Brief filed 'last week' per a press release dated 2023-05-24, so the filing date is in May 2023; the exact day is not stated.
subjects: minimum age to buy a gun

findings.passage: “We should not have to worry about mentally ill people getting their hands on an AR-15,” said AG Kris Mayes.
findings.note: Quoted by Arizona's Family (3TV/CBS 5), published 2023-10-30, in a report on her plan for a school-focused extreme-risk order law.
subjects: limits on who may have a gun

findings.passage: “Our office has been looking at crafting and helping to get introduced a ‘red flag’ law for Arizona,” she said.

“This particular proposal has a lot of due process built into it. It has a judge who has to make this determination; only a specific list of people are allowed to make these claims and ask for these orders, and it ultimately ends up in a hearing,” she said.
findings.note: Quoted by Arizona's Family (3TV/CBS 5), published 2023-10-30, describing safeguards in her proposed school-focused extreme-risk order.

findings.passage: My office has seen firsthand the devastation these weapons cause in our communities. Under current law, traffickers have been able to exploit loopholes and avoid serious prison time. HB 2131 changes that. This bill ensures that anyone who engages in weapons trafficking to gangs, criminal syndicates, or racketeering enterprises will face enhanced penalties.
findings.note: Statement of the Attorney General in her office's press release after the House passed HB 2131, a bill her office proposed.

Her office proposed HB 2131 (sponsored by a House member), which expands the weapons-trafficking offense to include transfer of even one weapon to assist organized criminal activity and bars probation for trafficking three or more weapons. She did not sponsor it; the page names Rep. Quang Nguyen as sponsor. Recorded as 'other' (office-proposed bill, publicly urged the Senate to pass it).
